findings.heading: General syntax
findings.proposition: English names the third argument of the join functions as `by = `; the translation names it `y = `, which is not an argument of `left_join()` and does not appear in the adjacent code chunk (`left_join(df1, df2, by = c("ID" = "identifier"))`).
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looks for an argument called `y` in the join functions, does not find it in `?left_join`, and cannot connect the prose to the `by =` argument used in every join example on the page.

findings.heading: Left and right joins
findings.proposition: English says the two new columns `catchment_pop` and `level` were added on the LEFT side of `linelist_mini`; the translation says they were added on the RIGHT side (`linelist_mini` の右側に).
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told the opposite of the English about where joined columns appear. The Japanese statement matches the actual `left_join()` output, so a reader comparing the two language versions cannot tell which is correct.

findings.heading: Inner join
findings.proposition: English introduces the example as the output of an `inner_join()` of `linelist_mini` with `hosp_info`; the translation says the output comes from `full_join()` (完全結合), while the code chunk immediately below runs `inner_join()`.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader in the inner-join section is told the demonstrated result is a full join, so the bullet points about dropped non-matching rows appear to contradict the named function, and the reader may believe `full_join()` removes non-matching rows.

findings.heading: Probabilistic deduplication
findings.proposition: English says the two rows ADDED to make `cases_dup` are the possible duplicates, i.e. "Tony" duplicates "Anthony" and "Maria Rodriguez" duplicates "Marialisa Rodrigues"; the translation reverses the first pair, saying the row "Anthony Smith" was added as a duplicate of "Tony Smith".
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reading the `cases_dup` chunk (row 2 is "Anthony", added row 10 is "Tony") sees the prose contradict the data, and mis-identifies which record is the original and which is the suspected duplicate when interpreting the `dedupe.ids` output.

findings.heading: Probabilistic deduplication
findings.proposition: English says to run `fastLink()` comparing the `cases_dup` data frame TO ITSELF; the translation says to run `fastLink()` and compare its OUTPUT with the `cases_dup` data frame (出力結果を `cases_dup` データフレームと比較します).
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told to compare a result object against the data frame, which is not what the adjacent chunk does (`dfA = cases_dup, dfB = cases_dup`), and misses the rule that deduplication is triggered by passing the same data frame twice.

findings.heading: Pre-cleaning
findings.proposition: English advises converting the VALUES of a column to all lowercase or all uppercase before a join; the translation advises converting the COLUMN NAMES (列名をすべて小文字または大文字に変換する).
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may rename columns instead of case-standardising the values that the join matches on, leaving the case-sensitivity problem the paragraph exists to prevent; the very next sentence then contradicts it by referring to all values in a column.

findings.heading: Bind columns
findings.proposition: English says `bind_cols()` combines two data frames SIDEWAYS (horizontally); the translation says it combines them 縦向きに (vertically/lengthwise).
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may understand `bind_cols()` as stacking data frames one below the other, the same as `bind_rows()`, and so misunderstand why row order and positional matching matter in this section.

findings.heading: Hospital information data frame
findings.proposition: English describes the extra hospital information as the catchment population and the level of care; the translation describes it as 患者数 (the number of patients) and the level of care.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader interprets `catchment_pop` (values such as 1950280) as a patient count rather than the population served, which changes the meaning of the column in every joined table on the page.

findings.heading: Probabilistic matching
findings.proposition: English states the purpose of the alternative approach: to obtain only the "original" 9 records of `cases` with the new column(s) from `results`. The translation states only that you may want to add specific columns, and omits the 9-record result.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn what distinguishes this second approach from the first (a 9-row result rather than one carrying all columns of both data frames), so cannot tell which approach to choose.

findings.heading: Probabilistic matching
findings.proposition: The translation names the columns to keep as `rowname` 列と `results` 列; the adjacent code chunk selects `select(rowname, result)`, and `results` is the name of the data frame, not of a column in it.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who follows the prose writes `select(rowname, results)`, which errors because no column `results` exists.

findings.heading: Anti join
findings.proposition: English lists troubleshooting SPELLING in a join as a common use of an anti-join; the translation keeps only the parenthetical idea of reviewing records that should have matched, and drops the spelling motivation.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader loses the main diagnostic use of an anti-join for exact-match joins, namely finding values that failed to match because of spelling differences, which is the problem the Pre-cleaning section earlier set up.

findings.heading: **dplyr** joins
findings.proposition: English credits the gifs with a link to https://github.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain/tree/master/images; the translation's link target is the malformed URL https://github.com/gadenbuieに感謝します。 (Japanese text merged into the address).
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who clicks the credit link reaches a non-existent page instead of the tidyexplain image repository, and cannot find the source of the join animations used throughout the chapter.

findings.heading: Semi join
findings.proposition: The translation adds a statement not present in the English segment: that `hosp_info` is the baseline data frame and `linelist_mini` is the secondary data frame, and names the join columns `hosp_name` and `hospital`.
findings.reader_consequence: No factual harm: the added statement agrees with the code. A Japanese reader gets an explicit baseline/secondary framing that English readers must infer, so the two versions differ in what the reader is told at this point.
